prompt.context: Our client is an upscale restaurant in TianJin, China. It serves government officials and high-level business customers. Its monthly revenue is 1.2M Yuan. The CEO recently hired us to help them increase their profitability.
prompt.question: How should the client increase its profitability?

clarifying_info.q: How is the upscale dining market growing?
clarifying_info.a: China's economy is booming; the upscale dining market is growing 20% per year
Customers for high-end dining are generally price insensitive
All competitors are earning money; price and value proposition are similar
Variable costs across the industry are 50% of revenue. Assume no fixed costs

clarifying_info.q: How is demand for individual rooms on weekdays?
clarifying_info.a: On weekdays, there is always a line for individual rooms

exhibits.title: Room and Pricing Data
exhibits.shows: Two side-by-side tables comparing Individual Rooms (20 tables) and Big Rooms (20 tables), broken down by Weekday and Weekend for both Lunch and Dinner. Each cell shows Occupancy rate, Price per person, and Party size per table.

framework: Revenue: Break down by room type (individual vs. big), time of day (lunch/dinner), and day of week (weekday/weekend); analyze occupancy, price per person, party size, and product mix
Revenue drivers: Identify which room type and time slot generates the most revenue; note that individual rooms at dinner/weekday are at 100% occupancy, signaling unmet demand
Customer segmentation: Government officials and business customers prioritize privacy, making individual rooms far more valuable to them than big rooms
Pricing power: Assess price sensitivity; market is price insensitive and growing 20% YoY; individual room weekday demand exceeds supply
Costs: Variable costs are 50% of revenue; no fixed costs; profit = 50% of revenue
Competition: All competitors are profitable; pricing and value proposition are similar — no competitive disadvantage
Potential solutions: (1) Raise prices on individual rooms; (2) Convert big room tables to individual rooms to capture unmet demand

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, identify the key issue in the current revenue structure.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates note that individual rooms are at 100% weekday dinner occupancy (demand fully constrained) while big rooms are significantly underutilized (20-30% weekday occupancy). Government and business customers prefer individual rooms for privacy. The restaurant is not meeting demand and is leaving revenue on the table. Two actions follow: raise individual room prices (customers are price insensitive) and convert underutilized big room tables into individual rooms.

questions.prompt: What are potential solutions to increase profitability?
questions.guidance: Two primary approaches: (1) Raise prices on weekday individual rooms — demand exceeds supply, customers are price insensitive, so a price increase loses little volume. (2) Convert some big room tables into individual rooms — big rooms are severely underutilized on weekdays while individual room demand is unmet. Exceptional candidates will propose both and evaluate them together.

questions.prompt: Market research shows that raising the weekday individual room price by 33% will cause a 10% customer loss. How will this change profitability?
questions.guidance: Calculate incremental daily profit from the price increase for both lunch and dinner, then scale to monthly. Use the exhibit data for occupancy and party size. Note that underlying demand is ~200% of capacity, so the price increase will not actually reduce volume in practice — this is a key insight.

math.setup: Individual Rooms: 20 tables. Weekday Lunch: 80% occupancy, 4 people/table, price Y150. Weekday Dinner: 100% occupancy, 6 people/table, price Y300. Variable cost = 50% of revenue. Price increase = +33%. Customer loss = 10%.
steps: Weekday Lunch — Previous customers: 20 * 80% * 4 = 64. New customers: 64 * 90% = 57.6 ≈ 58. Previous price: Y150. New price: 150 * 1.33 = Y200. Previous revenue: 64 * 150 = Y9,600. New revenue: 58 * 200 = Y11,600. Previous profit: 9,600 * 50% = Y4,800. New profit: 11,600 * 50% = Y5,800. Incremental profit: Y1,000.

Weekday Dinner — Previous customers: 20 * 100% * 6 = 120. New customers: 120 * 90% = 108 ≈ 120 (demand is 200% of capacity, so no actual loss). Previous price: Y300. New price: 300 * 1.33 = Y400. Previous revenue: 120 * 300 = Y36,000. New revenue: 120 * 400 = Y48,000. Previous profit: 36,000 * 50% = Y18,000. New profit: 48,000 * 50% = Y24,000. Incremental profit: Y6,000.
Daily incremental profit: Y1,000 + Y6,000 = Y7,000. Monthly (20 weekdays): 7,000 * 20 = Y140,000/month.
Key insight: Since underlying demand is 200% of capacity, the 10% loss assumption is theoretical — actual volume will not decline. The upside is even higher.
math.answer: Raising weekday individual room prices by 33% increases monthly profit by approximately Y140,000, assuming 20 weekdays/month.

questions.prompt: A second solution is converting half of the big room tables (10 tables) into 5 individual rooms. The renovation takes two weeks, during which the entire restaurant closes. Conversion costs Y100,000. What is the total project cost?
questions.guidance: Total cost = capital investment + opportunity cost (revenue lost during closure). Opportunity cost = monthly revenue * 50% variable cost ratio * 50% of month (2 weeks = half month). The observant candidate uses the initial monthly revenue figure (Y1.2M) directly rather than re-deriving from the table.

math.setup: Capital investment = Y100,000. Closure = 2 weeks = 0.5 months. Monthly revenue = Y1.2M (given in case prompt). Profit margin = 50%.
steps: Total project cost = Y100,000 + Y300,000 = Y400,000
math.answer: Total project cost = Y400,000 (Y100,000 capital + Y300,000 opportunity cost).

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential solutions for increasing profitability at this upscale restaurant?

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Raise weekday individual room prices (demand exceeds supply, customers price insensitive)
Introduce premium pricing tiers or private dining packages

categories.name: Capacity Reallocation
ideas: Convert underutilized big room tables into individual rooms
Phase conversion to minimize closure time and lost revenue
Create hybrid rooms convertible between individual and big-room configurations

categories.name: Revenue Mix
ideas: Shift menu toward higher-margin items (alcohol, premium dishes)
Introduce private dining packages for corporate clients
Add weekend promotions to boost low weekend occupancy in individual rooms

categories.name: Demand Management
ideas: Implement reservations system to better capture unmet weekday demand
Waitlist management for individual rooms to quantify lost revenue
Market more aggressively to government/business clients for weekday bookings

categories.name: Cost Optimization
ideas: Optimize staffing to match actual occupancy patterns (lower weekday lunch vs. dinner)
Reduce food waste given low big-room occupancy
Renegotiate vendor contracts given low big-room utilization

recommendation: Pursue both levers simultaneously: (1) Raise weekday individual room prices by 33% to capture Y140,000/month in incremental profit; demand is 200% of capacity so volume loss is minimal. (2) Convert half of big room tables into individual rooms at a total project cost of Y400,000, unlocking substantial long-term revenue from currently unmet demand.
Prioritize the price increase first as it requires no capital and delivers immediate monthly profit uplift.
risks: Renovation closure (2 weeks) creates short-term revenue disruption and reputational risk if key clients are turned away
If underlying demand softens (e.g., government austerity policies), the price increase could reduce volume more than modeled
Converting big rooms eliminates ability to serve large-party clients, potentially narrowing customer base
next_steps: Model long-term ROI of room conversion: estimate monthly incremental profit from new individual rooms vs. Y400,000 investment to determine payback period
Evaluate whether both solutions should be implemented together or sequentially
Assess regulatory or reputational risk of targeting government officials as primary clientele
Explore weekend occupancy improvement strategies to further increase revenue
